title: My honest experience vibe trading with AI (the compiler is the whole product)
author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
selftext:
I've been vibe trading with AI while building the layer that is supposed to stop it from lying. Different seat than a year of live systems. Same hangover.



People dump seven different jobs on a model and then argue about "AI trading". The argument is fake. Those are not the same job. The split that actually mattered for me is three.



1. The model trades, or picks direction.

2. The model writes the strategy. You own the test.

3. The model also grades the test.



1 is noise. Last month's best agent is a regime artifact. I stopped running that experiment.



3 is how you lose months. Same session proposes the spec, runs fifty variants, keeps the survivor, then writes you a PM memo. The backtest is not lying. The selection is. "Are you sure?" just makes it flip. Now you have two stories and no test.



2 is the only one I have seen hold up, and only if the grade cannot be negotiated.



What does not work:



\> "Claude, build me something that looks good on this CSV." It will. It will also have tested forty variants on the same window. You selected with the holdout even if the model never trained on it.



\> Letting the writer of the strategy decide whether it passed. Throughput is what burns the holdout. An automated loop is the most dangerous version of this, not the safest.



\> Counting only the runs that beat the previous best. The model saw the failures too. Those count. Bailey and Lopez de Prado assume you log every look. An LLM loop that mutates from the current winner is not a grid, so the independent-trial correction matters, but dropping the losers from N is how you launder the search.



\> Training a transformer on public data and calling it an edge. You paid GPU rent to overfit a dataset everyone else already used.



\> Looking for the one method, one asset, one prompt that prints. If the search is wide enough, something will look clean. That is the definition of the problem.



What does work:



\> Write a rule. Freeze the spec. Grade it on data the search never saw, with a trial counter that includes discards. If it dies, it dies. You do not get to prompt it back to life on the holdout.



\> LLM as the engineer. Specs, factor ideas, the plumbing. Not the trader. Not the referee.



\> Classical ML on top of a rule that already stands without it. Purged CV, walk forward, then still treat it as experimental. ML does not invent the edge. It sizes one you already had.



\> Paper after the holdout, not instead of it. Time is a filter. It is a slow one. Use it on the things that already survived, or you will paper-trade your way through another search.



Vibe coding works because the compiler tells you no, immediately, every time. Vibe trading has no compiler. The market takes months

comments.author: AcanthocephalaNo6605
comments.body:
You have a solid point and I can't agree more.

Couple of my friends and professional traders I talked to told me the same thing that they don't find alpha LLM trading for them. Its like a system without checks and ultimately it will fail one day.

One more thing I believe is, determinism and speed are non negotiable characteristics of financial markets and unfortunately LLM have non of them.

Your approach is on point. Use LLM to design the script or monitor the market or even do the analysis but don't allow it to trade for you. 

I know this is going to sound like an advertisement but still because topic is on point I would still like to mention that to resolve this approach for traders (who don't know coding or how to plug in brokers and data feeds) we have made while25, its agentic trading terminal where you have native python sdk to design your indicator strategy or even custom analysis. Everything is modular and you can do anything but trade using AI Assistant (the whole point)

You can check it out on while25.com

comments.body:
https://chatgpt.com/share/6a7d213c-47b4-83ea-8ab0-a2f2ad5a35f5

My process is tedious but it’s structured to avoid the defects you mentioned. I employ a layered governance stack - the layers are master spec, trade/execution spec, data/model spec, evaluation spec, risk/governance, decision control, configuration control, assurance case/claim-evidence matrix, independent verification/adversarial review (cross-model, Claude is well suited for this role with his hall monitor tone and excessive caveats), approval/authority, implementation evidence, operational/evaluation records, and project continuity/canon.

Chat picked up on a methodological watch item from your post so I added it to my project canon, thanks.
